name: ColorBench
ability_definition: The ability to match or detect differences between colors, including shades of color and brightness.

task_realism.reasoning: Several tasks map directly onto the core of the ability: Color Comparison, Color Extraction (RGB/HSV), Color Recognition and Ishihara-style plates. These resemble the perceptual acts behind workplace color matching and difference detection. Real work adds more, though: matching paint or dye lots, textile and print QC, inspecting wiring color codes, judging produce ripeness, spotting skin-tone changes. Those tasks happen on physical objects under specific lighting, with fine tolerances like Delta-E thresholds and a practical decision attached. Illusion, counting and proportion tasks move further away from actual job tasks.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Testing uses static digital images at a single pass, with no control over illuminant, display calibration, viewing angle or metamerism. There is no chance to re-inspect under different light, no reference swatches or instruments, and no stakes or tolerance specification. The inputs mix synthetic stimuli with curated real images, which only partly matches the input distribution of real work. The human baselines are useful but were collected under the same artificial conditions.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers hue recognition, fine color comparison, value extraction, color-blindness plates and illusion robustness, which is the broadest color-specific coverage available. Brightness and shade discrimination is not isolated, even though the O*NET definition names it explicitly. Some tasks (Proportion, Object Counting, Robustness) mix color with counting or reasoning skills. Matching a color to a reference sample under varying conditions is also underrepresented.

format_match.reasoning: All items are forced multiple-choice image-text questions. Real work outputs look different: a pass/fail QC judgment against a tolerance, a chosen matching swatch or formula adjustment, a graded description of a difference, or flagged defect regions. Multiple choice caps the precision being measured and lets models succeed by eliminating options rather than by continuous discrimination.

transferability_reasoning: ColorBench is the most construct-aligned benchmark for color discrimination, and several of its tasks directly probe hue and shade comparison, so it transfers better than general visual benchmarks. Transfer is limited by uncontrolled digital viewing conditions, the lack of isolated brightness testing, tasks that mix color with other skills, and a forced multiple-choice format unlike real color-matching and QC work. Strong scores would suggest basic color perception competence but would not guarantee reliable workplace color matching.

2025.metric: accuracy (%) on the Color Perception & Reasoning tasks combined (multiple-choice)
2025.human_reference: General adult workforce with normal color vision, i.e. people who match or discriminate colors in everyday work such as inspection, painting, retail or design support

2026.metric: accuracy (%) on Color Perception & Reasoning tasks, overall
2026.human_reference: General adult population with normal color vision (the typical worker who matches or detects color differences on the job, e.g., in retail, production or design support).
